question.value: What is the dust content and evolutionary stage of normal UV-selected star-forming galaxies at 4.4 < z < 5.9, and what is the cosmic dust mass density at z ~ 5?

evidence.quote: The dust content of normal galaxies and the dust mass density (DMD) at high-z (z > 4) are unconstrained given the source confusion and the sensitivity limitations of previous observations.
We have focused on the dust scaling relations and, by comparing them with predictions from chemical evolution models, we have probed the evolutionary stage of UV-selected galaxies at high-z.
The ALPINE targets were observed during Cycle 5 and Cycle 6 in Band 7 (275-373 GHz) which covers the [CII] line from z = 4.1 - 5.9.
In the ALPINE survey, 57 sources were also serendipitously detected at 860-1000 um (ALMA band-7)

frequencies_and_spectral_setup.value: 275-373 GHz covering [CII] 158 um and rest-frame ~157-158 um continuum

evidence.quote: The ALPINE targets were observed during Cycle 5 and Cycle 6 in Band 7 (275-373 GHz) which covers the [CII] line from z = 4.1 - 5.9.

We anticipate here that in Sec. 5.1 we will perform a stacking analysis on the rest-frame 157 um ALMA continuum images, including both the 23 individual continuum detected sources and the non-detections.
The goal of the ALPINE survey was to observe the prominent [CII] 158 um emission line for 118 UV-selected normal star-forming galaxies at z ~ 4.4 - 5.8.
The continuum maps - that are of interest for this work - were produced using line free channels, reaching an angular resolution between 0.7'' and 1.6''

evidence.quote: and mean sensitivities (RMS of 50 uJy/beam and 28 uJy/beam in the 4.3< z < 4.6 and 5.1< z < 5.9 ranges, respectively.
Each target was observed between 15 and 45 minutes.
The ALPINE targets were observed during Cycle 5 and Cycle 6 in Band 7 (275-373 GHz)

in this work we take advantage of our recently completed ALMA Large program to INvestigate [CII] at Early times (ALPINE, PI: Le Fèvre, see Le Fèvre et al. 2020, Béthermin et al. 2020, Faisst et al. 2020b).

evidence.quote: The model from Gioannini et al. (2017) is the one that best reproduces the global trend shown by the DMD evolution from the local Universe up to z ~ 5.

analysis_steps.goal: Derive dust masses for individual ALPINE continuum-detected targets, non-detections, and serendipitous sources

method.value: Single Modified Black Body (MBB) in optically thin regime evaluated at rest-frame 250 um (1.2 THz), extrapolated from observed Band 7 (rest-frame ~157 um) continuum flux

evidence.quote: We derive the dust masses using a single Modified Black Body (MBB) curve, under the approximation of an optically thin regime (see Bianchi 2013)

Dust masses are measured from the continuum emission at 250 um (see Gilli et al. 2014), extrapolated from the 157 um ALMA data, assuming a mass-weighted temperature of 25 K and a dust emissivity of beta=1.8

key_parameters.value: T = 25 K (fiducial), tested T = 20 K to 35 K

evidence.quote: For the temperature of the dust, we assume T= 25 K.
For the temperarure of the cold dust, we explore a range of values, from T=20 K up to T=35 K.

key_parameters.value: k_nu0 = 4 cm^2 g^-1 at nu0 = 1.2 THz (lambda_rest = 250 um), beta = 1.8

evidence.quote: We adopt k_nu0 = 4 cm^2 g^-1 with nu0 =1.2 THz (see Bianchi 2013) and beta = 1.8, i.e. the Galactic value from the Planck data (Planck Collaboration et al. 2011).

assumptions.value: Optically thin dust emission at rest-frame 250 um

evidence.quote: Considering the rest-frame frequency assumed to compute S_nu_obs, we have considered 1.2 THz, corresponding to lambda_rest = 250 um (see Gilli et al. 2014). At this wavelength our galaxies are expected to be optically thin

assumptions.value: Single diffuse cold dust component dominates the dust mass budget

evidence.quote: The adopted method relies on the assumption that the diffuse cold dust component accounts for the bulk of the dust budget.

assumptions.value: LambdaCDM cosmology with Omega_m = 0.3, Omega_lambda = 0.7, H_0 = 70 km s^-1 Mpc^-3

evidence.quote: Throughout the paper, we assume a LambdaCDM cosmology with Omega_m = 0.3, Omega_lambda = 0.7 and H_0 =70 km s^-1 Mpc^-3.

fitting.value: Analytical evaluation of single MBB equation; error bars computed by summing in quadrature relative uncertainties on 157 um flux (~25%), beta (~15%), and band conversion (~30%)

evidence.quote: We calculate the error bars on the dust masses by summing in quadrature the relative uncertainties on the 157 um continuum flux (~25%), the systematic uncertainties due to the beta emissivity (~15%) and to the band conversion emissivity (~30%).

validation.value: Tested sensitivity to beta (1.5 to 2.0 changes mass by <15%), temperature (T=20 K changes by 20%, T=35 K decreases by 60%), and rest-frame reference wavelength (250 um vs 850 um gives unchanged masses)

evidence.quote: we test how extreme values of beta=1.5 (beta=2) would affect our dust mass estimates finding an increase (decrease) of the dust masses by a negligible factor of less than ~15% for beta=1.5 (beta=2)
A temperature of T=20 K would increase the dust masses by a factor within the uncertainties considered (20%), while assuming T=35 K would produce a decrease of the order of 60%.
In fact, we have tested that our dust masses do not change if one considers 250 or 850 um and if the flux S_nu_obs in Eq. 1 is derived by means of an extrapolation at higher frequencies.

analysis_steps.goal: Compare observed dust scaling relations with chemical evolution models

method.value: Compare M_dust, M_gas, SFR, M_stars, and age of the 23 continuum-detected targets (and SFR vs age for non-detections) against chemical evolution tracks for proto-spheroids (PSPH) and spiral galaxies

evidence.quote: In Fig. 2 we compare estimates derived for the galaxies of our sample with results obtained with the chemical evolution models presented in Sect. 4.1.

key_parameters.value: PSPH final baryonic masses of 3e10, 1e11, and 1e12 M_sun; spiral final stellar masses from 2e9 to 1e11 M_sun

evidence.quote: The models describe three PSPH of final baryonic mass 3 x 10^10 M_sun, 10^11 M_sun and 10^12 M_sun.
The final stellar masses of the spirals range from 2 x 10^9 M_sun to 10^11 M_sun.

assumptions.value: Rescale observed M_stars and SFR from Chabrier (2003) IMF to Salpeter (1955) IMF by multiplying by 1.7

evidence.quote: For consistency with the models, we rescale M_stars and SFR to a Salpeter (1955) IMF by multiplying the quantities by a factor of 1.7 (see Speagle et al. 2014).

assumptions.value: PSPH models tested with Salpeter (1955) IMF and Larson (1998) top-heavy IMF (m_c = 1.2 M_sun); spiral models use Scalo (1986) IMF

evidence.quote: The stellar initial mass function (IMF) assumed for spirals is the one of Scalo (1986)
For the IMF of PSPH we test two different forms, i.e. the Salpeter (1955) IMF and the one of Larson (1998), a top-heavy IMF (THIMF).

validation.value: Checked against age of the Universe at z = 4.5 and 5.5, independent morphological classifications (Le Fèvre et al. 2020), and continuum non-detections in the SFR-age plane

evidence.quote: In fact, in the extreme and unlikely case that the ages are all systematically underestimated, they can not be larger than the age of the Universe at the redshift of our sample
A further indication supporting our conclusion, is the galaxy classification of the ALPINE targets, performed by Le Fèvre et al. (2020)
In Fig. 2 (panel c)), we report the SFR as a function of the age also for the ALPINE galaxies not detected in continuum (empty squares).

analysis_steps.goal: Stack ALMA continuum images in redshift and UV luminosity bins

method.value: Median stacking of rest-frame 158 um continuum images centered on UV counterpart positions, including both detections and non-detections, split into two redshift bins (z < 5 and z > 5) and three L_UV bins (~20 sources per bin)

evidence.loc: 5.1. Contribution to the DMD from UV-selected galaxies
evidence.quote: We perform stacking using the lambda_158um rest-frame continuum images centered on the UV counterpart positions, including both individual detections and non-detection in order to avoid biases.

evidence.loc: 5.1. Contribution to the DMD from UV-selected galaxies
evidence.quote: We use median stacking on the UV counterpart positions of both detected and non detected objects.

evidence.loc: 5.1. Contribution to the DMD from UV-selected galaxies
evidence.quote: We performed the stacking in two redshift bins, at z < 5 and z> 5, and we further split the sample in bins of UV luminosity.

key_parameters.value: Detection threshold 3.5 sigma; 3 sigma upper limits for non-detections (3 * background RMS + local maximum); L_UV bins: 10.4-10.9, 10.9-11.1, 11.1-11.6 log(L_sun)

evidence.loc: 5.1. Contribution to the DMD from UV-selected galaxies
evidence.quote: As for the detections, we adopt a 3.5sigma threshold. In case of non detection, we use the conservative 3sigma upper limits by adding three times the background RMS to the local maximum (see Béthermin et al. 2020.)

assumptions.value: Same MBB parameters (T = 25 K, beta = 1.8) applied to stacked fluxes and 3 sigma upper limits to derive M_dust

evidence.loc: 5.1. Contribution to the DMD from UV-selected galaxies
evidence.quote: For the non-detections and for the stacked images, the same procedure adopted for the detected sources has been used to estimate the dust masses, considering the 3sigma flux upper limits and the stacked results as rest-frame 158 um continuum fluxes, respectively.

analysis_steps.goal: Fit M_dust-L_UV and M_dust-L_IR scaling relations and compute cosmic dust mass density (DMD)

method.value: Bayesian linear regression of log(M_dust) vs log(L_UV) (on stacked data including upper limits) and log(M_dust) vs log(L_IR) (on 10 serendipitous sources), followed by convolution of the linear-space mean relation with the UVLF (Ono et al. 2018) and IRLF (Gruppioni et al. 2020)

evidence.loc: 5.1. Contribution to the DMD from UV-selected galaxies
evidence.quote: Following Khusanova et al. (2020a) (see also Fontana et al. 2004, Pozzi et al. 2020), we estimate the comoving density of our physical property by convolving the volume density of the proxy with the mean M_dust-L_UV relation

evidence.loc: 5.2. Contribution to the DMD from FIR blind detected galaxies
evidence.quote: As for the DMD obtained for the UV-galaxy population, we estimate the comoving density of our physical parameter (rho_dust,IR, where now the subscript IR stands for derived from IR-selected sources) by convolving the volume density of the proxy (L_IR) with the M_dust-L_IR relation

key_parameters.value: UVLF integration ranges: 10.4 < log(L_UV) < 11.5 (sampled lower limit) and 0.03 L* to 100 L* (full); IRLF integration ranges: 11.2 < log(L_IR) < 13 (sampled lower limit) and 9 < log(L_IR) < 14 (full)

evidence.loc: 5.1. Contribution to the DMD from UV-selected galaxies
evidence.quote: we estimate two quantities: the dust mass density derived by integrating the UV-luminosity only over the ALPINE UV-luminosity range and the dust mass density obtained by extrapolating the relation down to fainter UV luminosity not sampled by the ALPINE targets, and integrating over the commonly used 0.03L* - 100L* range (rho_dust,UV).

We also report in the second row the lower limits obtained by integrating the UVLF and IRLF only in the range sampled by the detected sources (10.4 <log(L_UV) < 11.5 and 11.2 <log(L_IR) < 13, respectively).

assumptions.value: ALPINE targets are representative of UV-selected galaxies at z ~ 5; conservative IRLF excluding 5 sources potentially in overdensities around central targets

evidence.loc: 5.1. Contribution to the DMD from UV-selected galaxies
evidence.quote: Two main caveats could affect our method and should be mentioned: first, we consider the ALPINE targets as a fair representative sample of the UV-sources

evidence.loc: 5.2. Contribution to the DMD from FIR blind detected galaxies
evidence.quote: Since these sources are possibly related to an overdensity (see also Lemaux et al. 2018, Loiacono et al. 2020 on this issue), we consider the conservative IRLF determination from Gruppioni et al. (2020), where these sources have been removed.

assumptions.value: Log-normal scatter correction exp(0.5 * (ln(10) * sigma)^2) applied when converting mean relation from log space to linear space

evidence.loc: 5.1. Contribution to the DMD from UV-selected galaxies
evidence.quote: In this operation we have converted the mean relation found in log space (see Fig. 4) to the mean relation in linear space as: < M_dust/L_UV >= 10^(<log M_dust/L_UV >+ 2.3xsigma^2/2)

fitting.value: Censored data likelihood (Feldmann 2019 / Kelly 2007) in LeoPy combined with MCMC sampler emcee

evidence.loc: 5.1. Contribution to the DMD from UV-selected galaxies
evidence.quote: We performed the fit using the method described in Feldmann (2019), for evaluating the likelihood in presence of censored data. This method is a generalization of the statistical approach of Kelly (2007) and is implemented in the LeoPy python package. The evaluation of the likelihood has been combined with a Bayesian tool to realize Monte Carlo Markov Chain for parameter space exploration, implemented in the emcee python package (Foreman-Mackey et al. 2013).

evidence.quote: The former has been computed considering the 1sigma uncertainty derived through the MCMC analysis of the IRLF estimated by Gruppioni et al. (2020) (see their Table 4).

findings_qualitative.value: ALPINE galaxies have dust masses, gas masses, and SFRs consistent with intermediate- and low-mass proto-spheroid (PSPH) chemical evolution models (precursors of local ellipticals or spiral bulges) rather than disc galaxy models.

evidence.quote: The comparison of the observed dust scaling relations with chemical evolution models suggests that ALPINE galaxies are not likely progenitors of disc galaxies, but of intermediate and low mass proto-spheroids, resulting in present-day bulges of spiral or elliptical galaxies.

findings_qualitative.value: A standard Salpeter IMF is generally sufficient to explain the dust masses of ALPINE galaxies in proto-spheroid models without requiring a top-heavy IMF, except for a couple of the most dust-massive galaxies.

evidence.quote: A couple of galaxies with particularly high M_dust are reproduced by the PSPH models with a THIMF (green dashed-dotted lines).

In most cases, a Salpeter IMF is sufficient to account for the observed dust masses, i.e. in general there is no particular need to invoke mechanisms such as a top-heavy IMF to enhance dust production

findings_qualitative.value: The cosmic dust mass density at z ~ 5 derived from UV-selected galaxies is ~30% of that derived from blind FIR-selected galaxies, demonstrating that UV selection misses the most dust-rich, UV-obscured galaxies.

evidence.quote: The DMD obtained at z ~ 5 from UV-selected sources is ~30 % of the value obtained from blind far-IR selected sources, showing that the UV-selection misses the most dust-rich, UV-obscured galaxies.

findings_qualitative.value: The phenomenological model of Gioannini et al. (2017) best reproduces the cosmic evolution of the dust mass density from z ~ 5 to the local Universe, whereas cosmological semi-analytical and hydrodynamic models overestimate the low-redshift (z < 1) dust mass density.

evidence.quote: The phenomenological model from Gioannini et al. (2017) is the model that best reproduces the observed evolution of rho_dust.

On the other hand, the ab-initio cosmological, semi-analytical models of Popping et al. (2017) and Vijayan et al. (2019) and and the cosmological simulations of Li et al. (2019) roughly account for the observed evolution of rho_dust dust at z > 1, but they overestimate the dust mass budget at lower redshift, failing in reproducing the decreasing trend observed at z < 1.

claims.hypothesis: UV-selected main-sequence star-forming galaxies at 4.4 < z < 5.9 are progenitors of proto-spheroids (bulges or ellipticals) rather than spiral discs.
claims.experiment: Derive dust masses for 23 ALPINE continuum-detected galaxies using a single MBB (T=25 K, beta=1.8) and compare their M_dust, M_gas, SFR, M_stars, and age against chemical evolution models for proto-spheroids and spirals.
claims.result: Observed dust masses (~10^8 M_sun at ages 0.1-0.5 Gyr) and SFRs match intermediate- and low-mass PSPH models, whereas spiral disc models require >1 Gyr to reach comparable dust masses; ~70% of continuum-detected galaxies also show disturbed morphologies.
claims.finding: ALPINE galaxies are likely progenitors of intermediate- and low-mass proto-spheroids (present-day bulges or ellipticals) rather than galaxy discs.

evidence.quote: The comparison of the observed dust scaling relations with chemical evolution models suggests that ALPINE galaxies are not likely progenitors of disc galaxies, but of intermediate and low mass proto-spheroids, resulting in present-day bulges of spiral or elliptical galaxies.
Typical dust mass values of ~ 10^8 M_sun as derived in the ALPINE sample of continuum detected sources are achievable already at early times (typically ~ 0.1-0.5 Gyr) in PSPH.

claims.hypothesis: UV-selected galaxy samples miss a substantial fraction of the cosmic dust mass budget at z ~ 5 compared to blind far-IR selections.
claims.experiment: Derive the dust mass density at z ~ 5 by convolving the stacked M_dust-L_UV relation of 118 UV-selected ALPINE targets with the UVLF, and compare it with the DMD derived by convolving the M_dust-L_IR relation of 10 serendipitous FIR-detected galaxies at 4.1 < z < 5.9 with the IRLF.
claims.result: log(rho_dust,UV) = 4.8 (+0.4/-1.0) M_sun Mpc^-3, which is ~30% of log(rho_dust,IR) = 5.3 (+0.5/-0.3) M_sun Mpc^-3 (marginally consistent within 1 sigma), and serendipitous sources have higher mean IR luminosity (<log L_IR> = 12.1 vs 11.6).
claims.finding: UV selection misses the most dust-rich, UV-obscured galaxies at z ~ 5, making the blind IR-derived DMD the more complete fiducial estimate.

evidence.quote: The DMD obtained at z ~ 5 from UV-selected sources is ~30 % of the value obtained from blind far-IR selected sources, showing that the UV-selection misses the most dust-rich, UV-obscured galaxies.

The derived rho_dust,UV is ~30 % rho_dust,IR, although the two estimates are marginally consistent at 1sigma. Our result supports the conclusion that UV-selected galaxies miss the most obscured/dusty objects and we consider rho_dust,IR as our fiducial value.

claims.hypothesis: Current cosmological simulations and chemical evolution models accurately reproduce the cosmic evolution of the dust mass density from z ~ 5 to z = 0.
claims.experiment: Compare the ALPINE z ~ 5 DMD measurements and lower-redshift literature DMD compilations against predictions from phenomenological (Gioannini et al. 2017), semi-analytical (Popping et al. 2017; Vijayan et al. 2019), and hydrodynamic (Aoyama et al. 2018; Li et al. 2019) models.
claims.result: Gioannini et al. (2017) reproduces the global trend from z ~ 5 to z = 0 (a factor ~2.5 increase to z ~ 1-3 followed by a factor ~3 decline to z = 0), while semi-analytical and hydrodynamic models overestimate the DMD at z < 1 and Li et al. (2019) underestimates the z ~ 5 IR DMD by up to a factor of ~10.
claims.finding: Phenomenological chemical evolution models tied to the cosmic SFR history reproduce the observed DMD evolution, whereas ab-initio cosmological models fail to reproduce both the high-z and low-z decline simultaneously.

evidence.quote: The model from Gioannini et al. (2017) is the one that best reproduces the global trend shown by the DMD evolution from the local Universe up to z ~ 5.

On the other hand, the models from Aoyama et al. (2018) and Li et al. (2019) are based on cosmological hydrodynamic simulations. They are globally inconsistent with the data, severely overestimating the DMD at z < 1.

why_this_data.value: ALPINE provides the first statistically robust sample of 118 UV-selected normal star-forming galaxies at 4.4 < z < 5.9 with high sensitivity and spatial resolution, avoiding the source confusion of earlier FIR instruments.

evidence.quote: The dust content of normal galaxies and the dust mass density (DMD) at high-z (z > 4) are unconstrained given the source confusion and the sensitivity limitations of previous observations. The ALMA Large Program to INvestigate [CII] at Early Times (ALPINE), which targeted 118 UV-selected star-forming galaxies at 4.4<z<5.9, provides a new opportunity to tackle this issue for the first time with a statistically robust dataset.

why_this_method.value: Single optically thin cold MBB (T=25 K, beta=1.8) is used because cold diffuse dust dominates the total dust mass budget; median stacking is required to include the ~80% continuum non-detections without bias; proxy LF convolution is required because ALPINE is not a volume-limited sample.

evidence.quote: The adopted method relies on the assumption that the diffuse cold dust component accounts for the bulk of the dust budget.

evidence.loc: 5.1. Contribution to the DMD from UV-selected galaxies
evidence.quote: Among the 118 ALPINE targets, 23 sources (~ 20% of the sample) are far-IR continuum detected and, as a consequence, for deriving the average properties of the parent UV-selected population, we need to take into account also the contribution of the non-detected galaxies.

evidence.loc: 5.1. Contribution to the DMD from UV-selected galaxies
evidence.quote: since the ALPINE sample is not a volume-limited sample, to derive the comoving density of our physical property (M_dust), we use L_UV as proxy of M_dust

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Warmer mass-weighted dust temperature (T = 35 K instead of fiducial T = 25 K), which reduces derived dust masses and DMDs by 60%

evidence.quote: A temperature of T=20 K would increase the dust masses by a factor within the uncertainties considered (20%), while assuming T=35 K would produce a decrease of the order of 60%.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Alternative dust emissivity index values (beta = 1.5 and beta = 2.0 instead of 1.8), which change dust masses by less than ~15%

evidence.quote: we test how extreme values of beta=1.5 (beta=2) would affect our dust mass estimates finding an increase (decrease) of the dust masses by a negligible factor of less than ~15% for beta=1.5 (beta=2)

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Using SFR(SED) from UV/optical SED fitting instead of SFR(UV+IR), rejected because a few outliers have SFR(UV+IR) up to ~5 times higher than SFR(SED)

evidence.quote: Anyway, since there are few outliers for which SFR(UV+IR) results to be a factor up to ~5 higher than SFR(SED), we prefer to consider the SFR(UV+IR) in the present analysis to properly account for dust-obscured SFR.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Top-heavy IMF (Larson 1998) vs standard Salpeter (1955) IMF in proto-spheroid chemical evolution models

evidence.quote: For the IMF of PSPH we test two different forms, i.e. the Salpeter (1955) IMF and the one of Larson (1998), a top-heavy IMF (THIMF).

limitations_admitted.value: Single band observation (ALMA Band 7, rest-frame ~157 um) requires assuming a fixed dust temperature (T = 25 K) and emissivity (beta = 1.8) and extrapolating to 250 um; if cold dust is at T = 35 K, dust masses and DMDs decrease by 60%.

evidence.quote: Morever, we discuss the uncertainties on the derived dust masses related to three (non-independent) factors: the 'band-conversion', linked to the extrapolation of the 250 um flux from higher frequencies (i.e. 157 um), the emissivity beta and the temperature T.
As stated in Sec. 3, a warmer dust mass (T= 35 K) would reduce the DMDs by a factor of 60%.

limitations_admitted.value: Stellar ages derived from SED fitting are highly uncertain, though bounded by the age of the Universe at z ~ 4.5-5.5.

evidence.quote: We are aware that the age is one of the most uncertain parameters of the SED-fitting analysis (i.e., Thomas et al. 2017).

limitations_admitted.value: The linear fit of log(M_dust) vs log(L_UV) from stacked images has poor statistical significance (constrained at 1-2 sigma, p-value = 0.08) and must be extrapolated to fainter UV luminosities not sampled by ALPINE.

evidence.loc: 5.1. Contribution to the DMD from UV-selected galaxies
evidence.quote: The fit results with a poor significance level with the coefficient constrained at 1-2sigma (Pearson rank coefficient of 0.76 and p-value of 0.08, estimated considering all data as detections).

evidence.loc: 5.1. Contribution to the DMD from UV-selected galaxies
evidence.quote: Two main caveats could affect our method and should be mentioned: first, we consider the ALPINE targets as a fair representative sample of the UV-sources; second, we extrapolate to a broader L_UV range, the log(M_dust)-log(L_UV) relation found for 10.4 <log(L_UV) < 11.5.

limitations_admitted.value: The IR-selected DMD determination has large uncertainty (~0.3-0.5 dex, up to 50%) due to the small sample (10 sources, 5 after removing overdensity candidates) used to constrain the IRLF.

evidence.quote: The large uncertainty (up to 50%) affecting our determination of rho_dust for IR selected galaxies reflects the small sample used to estimate the IRLF.

referee_caveats_inferred: Rest-frame 158 um is near the peak of the dust SED rather than deeply on the Rayleigh-Jeans tail, making single-band dust mass estimates highly sensitive to the assumed mass-weighted dust temperature.

The log(M_dust)-log(L_UV) regression is fit to only 6 stacked points (2 of which are upper limits), resulting in large slope uncertainty (+0.68/-0.57) that strongly affects the extrapolation to 0.03 L*.

missing_for_reproduction: Exact continuum flux measurement method on the median-stacked images (e.g. peak pixel, aperture, or 2D Gaussian fit)
Table of the 10 serendipitous continuum sources (IDs, redshifts, fluxes, L_IR, and M_dust) used in Fig. 5
Numerical tables of the chemical evolution model tracks from Calura et al. (2008, 2014, 2017)
reproducibility.estimated_data_volume_inferred: ~1-10 GB (118 continuum maps and catalog tables from ALPINE)
reproducibility.score_reason: The MBB dust mass calculation for the 23 detected targets is fully analytic and easily reproducible from the published ALPINE catalog (Béthermin et al. 2020), and the Bayesian fitting tools (LeoPy, emcee) and luminosity functions are explicitly specified; however, reproducing the image stacking requires the 118 continuum maps and exact flux extraction details, and the 10 serendipitous source values and chemical evolution tracks are not tabulated in the paper.
reproducibility.rediscovery_reason: The ALPINE continuum catalog and maps are public, the MBB formula and parameters (T=25 K, beta=1.8, k_1.2THz=4 cm^2/g) are completely specified, and the paper provides an exact answer key for the 23 target dust masses (Table A.1), stacked dust masses (Table 1), scaling relation fits, and cosmic dust mass densities (Table 2).
